title: “THEY WILL NOT ENDURE SOUND TEACHING” — THE TERRIFYING WARNING PAUL GAVE ABOUT CHRISTIANS WHO ONLY WANT TO HEAR WHAT MAKES THEM FEEL GOOD
paragraphs: “THEY WILL NOT ENDURE SOUND TEACHING” — THE TERRIFYING WARNING PAUL GAVE ABOUT CHRISTIANS WHO ONLY WANT TO HEAR WHAT MAKES THEM FEEL GOOD
What if the greatest danger to your faith is not the preacher who openly denies Jesus, but the one who keeps mentioning His name while quietly removing everything He commanded you to surrender?
There is something frightening happening in Christianity today.
And the most frightening part is that many people no longer recognize it as dangerous.
A preacher stands before thousands. The music is beautiful. The atmosphere is emotional. People are crying. Hands are raised. The message is encouraging.
Everyone leaves feeling better.
But somewhere in the middle of all that excitement, something essential may have been missing.
Nobody was confronted with sin.
Nobody was called to repentance.
Nobody was reminded that following Jesus means denying yourself, taking up your cross, and following Him.
Nobody was told that forgiveness is freely offered through Christ, but that grace is never permission to make peace with the very sin from which He came to save us.
And the congregation loved the message.
They called it powerful.
They called it anointed.
They shared the clips.
They followed the preacher.
But here is the question that should make every one of us uncomfortable:
Did they encounter the truth of Jesus Christ, or did they simply hear a religious version of what they already wanted to believe?
Because almost two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul warned that a time would come when people would no longer tolerate sound teaching.
Not because they had never heard the truth.
But because they no longer wanted it.
Listen carefully to what he wrote.

“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.”
— 2 Timothy 4:3–4, KJV
Read that again.
Paul did not merely say that false teachers would appear.
He said people would actively gather teachers who suited their desires.
That distinction changes everything.
Because sometimes the greatest problem is not that someone is willing to preach a lie.
It is that an audience is willing to reward him for preaching it.
And before we point our fingers at churches, pastors, influencers, or denominations, we need to ask something far more personal.
What happens inside your heart when Scripture tells you something you do not want to hear?
Do you surrender?
Or do you start looking for another interpretation that will let you keep living exactly as you are?
That question is not comfortable.
It was never meant to be.
Paul's warning was not written to entertain Christians.
It was written to awaken them.
And perhaps the most dangerous person in this entire story is not the false teacher standing behind the pulpit.
Perhaps it is the person sitting in the congregation, holding a Bible, quietly deciding which parts of God's Word deserve obedience.
Perhaps, at certain moments, that person has been you.
Perhaps it has been me.
And that is precisely why we need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The original Greek makes Paul's warning even more penetrating.
In 2 Timothy 4:3, the expression translated “sound doctrine” is τῆς ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας (tēs hygiainousēs didaskalias).
The word hygiainousēs comes from a verb meaning to be healthy or sound. It describes teaching that is spiritually wholesome, reliable, and consistent with the truth.
Paul was not talking about teaching that simply sounds impressive.
He was talking about teaching that is healthy for the soul.
And that creates a powerful picture.
Imagine a doctor examining a patient whose condition is deteriorating.
The doctor discovers a serious illness.
But the patient does not want frightening news.
He wants reassurance.
He wants to hear that everything is fine.
He wants medicine that tastes sweet.
He wants someone to tell him he can continue every destructive habit without consequences.
So he leaves the honest doctor and searches for another.
Eventually, he finds one who smiles and says exactly what he wants to hear.
“You are perfectly healthy. There is nothing you need to change.”
The patient walks out relieved.
He feels wonderful.
He tells everyone how amazing his new doctor is.
But the disease is still spreading.
The comforting diagnosis did not make him healthy. It only made him less aware of his danger.
That is the spiritual tragedy Paul was describing.
A message can make you feel better without making you spiritually healthier.
A sermon can move your emotions without moving your heart toward repentance.
A preacher can inspire your dreams while never addressing your rebellion against God.
And a church can grow in attendance while individual hearts remain untouched by the transforming truth of the Gospel.
This does not mean every encouraging sermon is shallow, or every emotionally moving worship service is spiritually empty.
Scripture itself is filled with comfort, joy, hope, and promises of God's faithfulness.
But biblical encouragement never requires us to conceal biblical truth.

The same Jesus who said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28, KJV), also said, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24, KJV).
Both statements came from the same Savior.
We do not have permission to keep the invitation and erase the cross.
And here is where Paul's language becomes even more unsettling.
He wrote that people would gather teachers according to their own desires.
The Greek phrase is κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας (kata tas idias epithymias).
It means “according to their own desires.”
The word epithymias refers to strong desires or cravings, which in this context are directing people away from sound teaching.
In other words, their desires become the standard by which they select their teachers.
Not faithfulness to Scripture.
Not the truth about Jesus.
Not whether the message produces repentance, holiness, love, and obedience.
But whether the message agrees with what they already want.
Think about how easily that can happen.
You are in a relationship that repeatedly pulls you away from obedience to Christ.
You know something is wrong.
You have read the Scriptures.
Your conscience has been troubled.
But instead of asking God for the courage to obey, you begin searching for voices that will make the relationship feel spiritually acceptable.
Or perhaps bitterness has settled inside you.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone humiliated you.
Someone caused real pain.
And forgiveness feels impossible.
So you begin surrounding yourself with messages that justify permanent hatred, never seriously considering Christ's call to forgive.
Or perhaps money has become the center of your life.
Your worth rises and falls with your possessions.
Your security depends on your bank account.
And you begin embracing every message that presents God primarily as a means of achieving financial success.
Slowly, almost invisibly, something changes.
You are no longer allowing Scripture to examine your desires.
You are allowing your desires to determine which interpretations of Scripture you will accept.
That is not spiritual maturity.
That is spiritual self-deception.
And it can happen to anyone.
Even someone who has attended church for decades.
Even someone who knows Bible verses by memory.
Even someone who regularly posts Christian content.
Even someone who sincerely believes they love Jesus.
Because knowing religious language is not the same as submitting to the Lord who stands behind His Word.
Paul then uses another unforgettable expression.
κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν (knēthomenoi tēn akoēn).
Literally, the phrase conveys the idea of having the hearing tickled or itching.
This is where the familiar expression “itching ears” comes from.
The picture is not simply of people who enjoy listening.
It is of people whose appetite for hearing is being directed by what pleases them.
They want teachers who satisfy the itch.
Teachers who reassure them.
Teachers who affirm their preferred conclusions.
Teachers who will not disturb what they have already decided to protect.
And we need to understand something important.
False teaching does not always arrive wearing an obviously evil disguise.
Sometimes it arrives with a smile.
Sometimes it quotes Scripture.
Sometimes it speaks constantly about blessings, purpose, destiny, success, and favor.
Those subjects are not inherently unbiblical.
God truly blesses His people. He truly gives purpose. He truly comforts the brokenhearted.
The danger begins when these truths are detached from the whole counsel of God and used to replace the message of sin, the cross, repentance, faith, and new life in Christ.
A half-truth can become deeply misleading when it is presented as the whole truth.
And that is why discernment requires more than asking whether a preacher mentioned Jesus.
We must ask whether the Jesus being proclaimed is the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Savior who forgives sinners.
The King who calls His people to obedience.
The Shepherd who seeks the lost.
The Son of God who is full of grace and truth.
Not a Jesus reconstructed to agree with every passing cultural preference.
Not a Jesus who exists merely to approve our ambitions.
Not a Jesus who never challenges our idols.
But the real Jesus Christ.
And there is something deeply beautiful about the real Jesus that counterfeit versions can never reproduce.
He loves us too much to leave us enslaved to the things destroying us.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
Her story is recorded in John 8:1–11.
She was placed in the middle of a public confrontation.
Her shame was exposed.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
Imagine the fear.
Imagine the humiliation.
Imagine standing before a crowd knowing that your worst moment had become public knowledge.
Then Jesus spoke.
After challenging the accusers, He addressed the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Those words belong together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy and moral truth.
Compassion and a call to change.
Jesus did not join the crowd in destroying her.
But He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He refused both merciless condemnation and moral indifference.
He offered mercy without calling evil good.
That is the beauty of Christ.

And although this passage has a well-known textual history—it is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions—the distinction between grace and permission to sin is firmly established elsewhere in Scripture.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may increase.
Paul answers emphatically, “God forbid.”
Grace is not an excuse to remain captive.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us through Jesus Christ and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.”
Notice that.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace does not merely soothe the conscience while leaving the heart unchanged.
And this is where the Gospel becomes intensely personal.
Because many of us have had seasons when we wanted God's comfort but resisted His correction.
We wanted peace without confession.
Forgiveness without admitting what we had done.
Restoration without surrendering the habits that kept breaking us.
We wanted Jesus to remove the consequences while allowing us to protect the cause.
We wanted the crown without the cross.
But Jesus did not come merely to improve the appearance of our lives.
He came to save us from sin and reconcile us to God.
That salvation is not something we purchase through religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
And the very next verse says that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
We obey because the grace that saves us begins transforming us.
We are not made righteous before God by our ability to become perfect.
Our hope rests in the perfect righteousness, atoning death, and victorious resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And because He is alive, change is possible.
Not effortless.
Not always immediate.
But possible through His grace.
Perhaps you know what it means to struggle with a sin you promised never to repeat.
Perhaps you have prayed through tears, only to find yourself facing the same temptation again.
Perhaps you have hidden behind Christian language because you are terrified that people would reject you if they knew what was happening in your private life.
And perhaps the last thing you want right now is another message telling you that something needs to change.
But hear this carefully.
The truth that exposes your sin is not necessarily the voice of someone trying to destroy you. It may be the very truth God is using to lead you back to life.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation leaves you staring at your guilt without hope.
Godly conviction calls you to acknowledge your sin and turn toward the Savior who is able to forgive and restore.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That promise does not mean sin has become insignificant.
It means Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith finds a Savior who is mighty to save.
The Gospel is not that you are already good enough.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save sinners who could never make themselves good enough.
That is why sound teaching matters so much.
Because sound teaching brings us back to the true Christ.
Not merely to religious excitement.
Not merely to a better self-image.
Not merely to temporary motivation.
But to the Savior who died for our sins and rose for our justification.
Now consider what Paul said immediately before his warning about itching ears.
In 2 Timothy 4:2, he commanded Timothy:
“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.”
Notice the balance.
Reprove.
Rebuke.
Exhort.
With patience.
With teaching.
Paul did not command Timothy to become cruel, arrogant, or needlessly offensive.
He did not tell him to embarrass struggling believers.
He did not tell him to turn the pulpit into a weapon for personal anger.
He told him to preach the Word faithfully and patiently.
That matters because some people misunderstand the call to sound doctrine.
They assume that the harshest preacher must be the most faithful.
That the angriest sermon must be the most biblical.
That compassion is weakness.
That tenderness is compromise.
But Scripture rejects that distortion too.
Second Timothy 2:24–25 teaches that the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome, but gentle, patient, and able to teach, correcting opponents with gentleness.
Truth does not become more biblical simply because it is shouted.
And love does not become more genuine by refusing to tell the truth.
Jesus embodied both perfectly.
John 1:14 describes Him as “full of grace and truth.”
Not half grace and half truth.
Not grace on Sundays and truth on Mondays.
Full of both.
And that is the standard we desperately need.
Preachers who refuse to dilute Scripture.
Believers who refuse to confuse personal preferences with biblical authority.
Churches where wounded people can encounter real compassion without being told that repentance is unnecessary.
Communities where difficult questions are welcomed, Scripture is carefully explained, and Christ remains the center.
Because sound doctrine is not merely about winning theological arguments.
It is about knowing the true God.
And knowing Him changes how we live.
It changes how we treat our spouses.
How we raise our children.
How we handle money.
How we respond when someone wounds us.
How we behave when nobody is watching.
How we confess our failures.
How we love people who disagree with us.
How we endure suffering without abandoning hope.
And how we return to Christ when we fall.
This is why the warning in 2 Timothy 4 is not simply a prophecy to use against other Christians.
It is a mirror.
A mirror that asks whether we are teachable.
Whether we love the truth more than our own opinions.
Whether we are willing to be corrected by Scripture.
Whether we are willing to let the Holy Spirit expose what pride has been hiding.
And whether we still desire Jesus Himself more than the comfort of hearing that we are always right.
There is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
In 2 Timothy 4:4, Paul says people will turn away from the truth and turn aside to myths.
The Greek word translated “fables” in the KJV is μύθους (mythous), meaning myths or fabricated stories.
Paul's concern was not that people would enjoy storytelling.
It was that they would exchange divine truth for religious narratives that could not faithfully lead them to Christ.
And that danger has not disappeared.
Today, we can access thousands of sermons with a single touch.
We can listen to countless teachers without ever opening a Bible ourselves.
We can surround ourselves with voices that repeat our assumptions until those assumptions begin to feel unquestionably true.
We can mistake popularity for faithfulness.
Confidence for wisdom.
Emotional intensity for spiritual authority.
And viral reach for God's approval.
But a message does not become true because millions have watched it.
And a message does not become false simply because it is unpopular.
The question remains:
Is it faithful to the Word of God, understood in its proper context, and centered on the truth of Jesus Christ?
That question must also be applied to Gospel Warrior.
Yes, even to this article.
Do not believe something merely because it sounds powerful.
Do not accept a claim merely because it makes you cry.
Open your Bible.
Read the passages in context.
Examine the meaning.
Ask questions.
Test what is being taught.
The believers in Berea were commended in Acts 17:11 because they examined the Scriptures daily to see whether Paul's message was true.
If they examined the teaching of an apostle, how much more should we carefully examine every modern preacher, writer, ministry, and online Christian voice?
Including the ones we love.
Including the ones who inspire us.
Including the ones who say exactly what we want to hear.
Because our loyalty must ultimately belong to Jesus Christ, not to a personality, a platform, or a ministry brand.
And perhaps that is the hardest lesson of all.
Sometimes faithfulness requires us to admit that someone we admire has taught something incorrectly.
Sometimes it requires us to change a long-held opinion.
Sometimes it requires us to apologize to someone we have judged unfairly.
Sometimes it requires us to stop sharing a dramatic religious claim because we cannot verify that Scripture actually teaches it.
And sometimes it requires us to sit alone with an open Bible and confess:
“Lord, I have been listening for what I wanted to hear instead of asking what You have actually said.”
That prayer may not attract applause.
But it may mark the beginning of genuine spiritual renewal.
There is a scene from Peter's life that captures the beauty of Christ's restoring grace.
Peter had promised loyalty to Jesus.
He had spoken boldly.
He believed he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
Then the night of Jesus' arrest came.
Fear overwhelmed him.
And three times, Peter denied knowing the Lord.
The man who had spoken so confidently found himself confronted with his own weakness.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered the Lord's words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of his own denial still fresh in his memory.
The realization that he had failed the One he loved.
The shame.
The grief.
The unbearable knowledge that his confident promises had collapsed under pressure.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep, as recorded in John 21:15–19.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
He addressed Peter personally.
He called him to love.
He called him to serve.
He called him to follow.
The same Peter who had denied Jesus would later proclaim Him boldly.
Not because Peter had discovered some hidden strength within himself.
But because the risen Christ was not finished with him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our failures are imaginary.
Not that our sins do not matter.
Not that truth should be softened until it no longer challenges us.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem people whose failures are painfully real.
He can forgive the ashamed.
Restore the fallen.
Strengthen the weak.
Humble the proud.
And bring the wandering home.
That is more than a beautiful phrase.
It is the testimony of what Christ does in the lives of sinners.
But remember this.
Jesus does not rewrite our stories by declaring that darkness was light all along.
He rewrites them by bringing us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
He does not call us to hide our wounds beneath religious appearances.
He invites us to bring our brokenness to Him.
He does not promise that discipleship will always be comfortable.
He promises that He will be with His people.
And His grace is worth more than the temporary comfort of being told that nothing in our lives needs to change.
So perhaps today is the day to ask a different question.
Not, “Which preacher makes me feel the best?”
But, “Which teaching helps me understand Scripture faithfully and follow Jesus more closely?”
Not, “Which message confirms everything I already believe?”
But, “Lord, what have I misunderstood, and what do I need to surrender?”
Not, “How can I avoid conviction?”
But, “How can I respond to Your truth with humility, repentance, and faith?”
And if something in this article has touched a place you have been avoiding, do not rush past it.
Do not bury it beneath another video.
Do not distract yourself with another argument.
Bring it to Jesus.
You do not need to impress Him with religious language.
You do not need to pretend that your spiritual life is stronger than it is.
You can tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I have been selective with Your Word.”
“Lord, I have justified things You have called me to surrender.”
“Lord, I have mistaken emotional comfort for spiritual growth.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
And if you are genuinely struggling, remember that repentance is not the same as instant perfection.
The Christian life involves ongoing growth, confession, dependence, and perseverance.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness when we confess them.
Do not let the reality of your struggle convince you that returning to Jesus is pointless.
Return to Him.
Again, with genuine repentance.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Christ is merciful.
And because His mercy is powerful enough to transform lives.
Your story may encourage someone who believes their worst chapter must be their final chapter.
You do not have to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss. A sincere prayer or a few words of testimony can be enough.
Because behind every comment is a real person.
Someone carrying a burden.
Someone fighting temptation.
Someone searching for answers.
Someone who needs to know that the grace of Jesus Christ is not merely a theological idea.
It is living hope.
Not to prove that you are more spiritual than anyone else.
Not to attack a pastor or embarrass another believer.
But because someone in your circle may be confusing a comfortable message with a faithful one.
Someone may be drifting from Scripture without realizing it.
Someone may be wounded by harsh religion and need to discover that biblical truth and genuine compassion belong together.
Someone may have abandoned hope because they believe their failures have placed them beyond the mercy of God.
Invite your family, fellow believers, those who are questioning Christianity, and even those who have walked away from church to examine the claims of Christ for themselves.
Not because every sentence here deserves to be remembered, but because the Scriptures behind it deserve to be revisited.
Return to 2 Timothy 4.
Read the entire chapter.
Read 2 Timothy 3.
Read the Gospels.
Study how Jesus treated sinners, challenged hypocrisy, comforted the brokenhearted, and called people to follow Him.
Let God's Word—not the emotional force of any article—be the foundation of your convictions.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be a place where people simply consume emotional Christian content and move on.
Our desire is to build a community where believers are nourished by Scripture, challenged toward spiritual maturity, encouraged in their struggles, and continually directed back to Jesus Christ.
Those free resources are part of our commitment to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
And maintaining and expanding that work requires real time, resources, and support.
It is an opportunity to help sustain the work of creating and sharing Christ-centered resources, strengthening discipleship, and reaching more people with biblical truth.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
The Bible teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”

We also recognize that Christians understand and practice tithing differently, and that financial support for a digital ministry should not automatically be equated with a biblical tithe or replace responsibilities to one's local church, family, or those in genuine need.
Your generosity should flow from love for God, not pressure, guilt, or fear.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal encouragement, or meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that seeks to point people toward Jesus Christ.
To help someone encounter Scripture.
To encourage someone who is close to giving up.
To provide resources for someone who wants to grow in faith but does not know where to begin.
To remind someone burdened by shame that repentance and forgiveness are possible through the cross.
And to keep proclaiming that our hope is not found in religious performance, human popularity, or messages designed to satisfy itching ears.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
A person who cannot give financially is no less precious to Christ than someone who can.
The Gospel is not for sale.
We want to serve people with the truth of God's Word, while inviting those who are able to help us continue serving others.
Because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully.
Not edited to please an audience.
Not softened to protect a platform.
Not exaggerated to attract attention.
And not turned into a business transaction that promises God's blessings in exchange for money.
It must remain the Gospel.
The good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The good news that forgiveness is available through Him.
The good news that sinners can be reconciled to God.
The good news that repentance is not the end of hope, but the turning of a heart toward the Savior who alone can save.
And now, before you leave, remember how this entire conversation began.
Paul warned that people would no longer endure sound teaching.
They would seek teachers who satisfied their desires.
They would turn away from truth.
And they would embrace what their itching ears wanted to hear.
But you do not have to become that person.
You can choose to love the truth even when it corrects you.
You can choose to remain teachable.
You can choose to study Scripture rather than merely collecting favorite verses.
You can choose to listen carefully, test what you hear, and follow Jesus rather than personalities.
And when the Word of God exposes something you have been hiding, you can come into the light instead of running from it.
Because the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who stretched out His arms upon the cross.
The One who knows the worst truth about your sin is the One who gave His life to save sinners.
And the One who calls you to follow Him is the risen Lord who can sustain you by His grace.
So here is the question I hope you carry long after you close this article:
If Jesus told you the truth you least wanted to hear today, would you still follow Him tomorrow?
Do not answer too quickly.
Take that question into prayer.
Let it examine your loyalties.
Let it expose your excuses.
Let it remind you that genuine discipleship is not about finding a version of Jesus who agrees with everything you want.
It is about surrendering to the real Jesus, who is infinitely more worthy of your trust than your own desires.
Not as a performance for other people.
But as a simple expression of your desire to remain faithful to Christ.
Because one day, the applause will fade.
The trends will disappear.
The viral sermons will be forgotten.
The platforms will change.
But the Word of the Lord will endure forever.
And when everything else falls silent, what will matter is not how many voices told you what you wanted to hear.
It will be whether you listened to the One who spoke the truth that could save your soul.
The most loving voice in your life may be the one that refuses to bless the chains Jesus died to break.
